analysis.one_liner: Gives renters 90 days' notice before eviction when their landlord's home is foreclosed.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and never got a vote before the Congress ended, so renters facing eviction after a foreclosure got no federal protection.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2008 foreclosure wave, renters were being evicted with little or no notice because the building they lived in was foreclosed — even though they had paid rent on time. This bill would have required whoever took over a foreclosed property to honor the existing lease until it ended, or at least give the tenant 90 days' notice to leave. It also extended similar protections to renters in the Section 8 housing voucher program. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in foreclosed buildings. The bill would have let a tenant with a lease stay through its full term, and given tenants without leases at least 90 days to find new housing before they had to move. It also protected Section 8 voucher holders by keeping their assistance contracts in force for a new owner.

how_it_helps.text: Anyone who takes over a foreclosed home must give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate before the tenant has to leave [S2][S3].
A tenant with a valid lease signed before the foreclosure can stay through the end of the lease term, unless the new buyer will live in the unit as their own primary residence [S2][S3].

For Section 8 voucher tenants, a foreclosure does not by itself count as good cause to end the lease during the initial term, and the new owner inherits both the lease and the housing assistance contract [S2][S3].
The bill does not override state or local laws that give tenants longer or stronger protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, banks, and investors who acquire foreclosed homes. Instead of taking immediate possession and reselling with an empty unit, they would have to honor existing leases or pay tenants to leave early, which lowers what buyers will pay for occupied foreclosed properties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders and buyers of foreclosed homes

drawbacks.text: Successors in interest — often lenders or investors — would bear the cost: they cannot take prompt possession of a foreclosed unit and must either wait out the lease or negotiate with the tenant, which reduces the resale value of occupied foreclosed homes [S2][S3].

Skeptics of tenant protections in foreclosures argue that making foreclosed properties harder to resell slows the housing market's recovery and can lead to occupied units sitting vacant and deteriorating; the bill addresses this only partly, by allowing termination when a buyer will occupy the home as a primary residence [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to tenants is direct and large: it prevents the classic scenario of a rent-paying tenant being evicted on days' notice because of a dispute they had no part in. The cost falls on lenders and investors in the form of delayed possession and lower resale value, and those costs are partly passed into the price of foreclosed homes. On balance the protections are modest and well-targeted — a 90-day floor plus lease recognition is far short of the stronger state laws the bill explicitly preserves.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the bill on May 19, 2008, with Sen. Edward Kennedy as its cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders and investors who acquire foreclosed properties are better off, because they could keep taking quick possession and evicting tenants on whatever short notice state law allowed — which is exactly what was happening as foreclosures peaked.

for.name: Sen. John F. Kerry
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to give tenants in foreclosed buildings 90-day notice and lease protections.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Kerry's behalf on the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee never acted on the bill — no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape was never tested; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were both Democrats, but with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders, banks, and investors buying foreclosed homes
industries.note: They would have had to honor existing leases or give tenants 90 days before evicting, delaying resale of foreclosed properties and reducing what buyers pay for occupied units. Their interest in fast, empty possession ran directly against tenants' need for housing stability.

Ordinary landlords are largely unaffected — the bill only applies when a property changes hands through foreclosure. Owner-occupant buyers get an escape hatch: they can terminate a lease with 90 days' notice if they will live in the unit themselves.
